core: Timbre as tone color or tone quality
The role of overtones, sound production, and sound source in distinguishing tone color
Describing timbre with cautious, specific listening language
supporting: Separating timbre from pitch, dynamics, tempo, texture, and articulation
How materials, manner of production, and acoustic ambience can affect heard sound color
Comparing voices and instruments without treating metaphors as objective rankings
outOfScope: A mathematical treatment of spectra, Fourier analysis, or acoustic measurement
Medical claims about hearing or vocal health
Claims that sound descriptors have universal emotional meanings or fixed cultural values

claims.claim: Timbre is the tone color or tone quality of a sound.
Overtones above a fundamental pitch help give a note its distinctive sound; the balance of a fundamental and its overtones shapes timbre.
The materials of an instrument and the way its sound is produced can affect its timbre, allowing different sources to sound different even when they perform comparable pitches.
Listeners commonly use descriptive metaphors such as bright, dark, rough, smooth, breathy, metallic, gravelly, or warm to discuss timbre.
Timbre is distinct from dynamics, which concerns volume or loudness, and from pitch, which concerns perceived highness or lowness.
A responsible timbre description identifies audible features and context rather than treating a metaphor or personal response as an objective property of all listeners.
